title: Chapter 82 — The Honor and Glory of Whaling
paragraphs: There are some enterprises in which a careful disorderliness is the true method.

The more I dive into this matter of whaling, and the further I push my research up to its very source, the more I am impressed by its great honor and antiquity. And especially when I find so many great demigods and heroes, and prophets of every sort, who one way or another have brought it distinction, I am carried away by the thought that I myself belong, even if only in a humble rank, to a brotherhood so emblazoned with glory.

The gallant Perseus, a son of Jupiter, was the first whaleman; and to the eternal honor of our calling, let it be said that the first whale our brotherhood ever attacked was not killed for any sordid motive. Those were the knightly days of our profession, when we took up arms only to rescue the distressed, and not to fill men's lamp-feeders. Everyone knows the fine story of Perseus and Andromeda: how the lovely Andromeda, a king's daughter, was tied to a rock on the seacoast, and just as Leviathan was in the very act of carrying her off, Perseus, the prince of whalemen, fearlessly advanced, harpooned the monster, and rescued and married the maiden. It was an admirable, artful feat, and one the best harpooners of today rarely achieve, since this Leviathan was killed with the very first throw. And let no one doubt this Arkite story; for in ancient Joppa, now Jaffa, on the Syrian coast, there stood for many ages, in one of the pagan temples, the vast skeleton of a whale, which the city's legends and all its inhabitants declared to be the very bones of the monster Perseus killed. When the Romans took Joppa, that same skeleton was carried to Italy in triumph. What seems most remarkable and suggestively important in this story is this: it was from Joppa that Jonah set sail.

Related to the adventure of Perseus and Andromeda — indeed, some suppose it was indirectly derived from it — is the famous story of St. George and the Dragon. That dragon, I maintain, was a whale; for in many old chronicles whales and dragons are strangely jumbled together and often stand in for each other. "You are like a lion of the waters, and like a dragon of the sea," says Ezekiel — plainly meaning a whale; in fact, some versions of the Bible use that very word. Besides, it would take a great deal from the glory of the exploit if St. George had merely met a crawling reptile of the land, instead of doing battle with the great monster of the deep. Any man can kill a snake, but only a Perseus, a St. George, a Nantucket Coffin has the heart to march boldly up to a whale.

Don't let the modern paintings of this scene mislead us. It is true that the creature this valiant whaleman of old fought is vaguely shown in a griffin-like shape, and that the battle is pictured on land, with the saint on horseback. But consider the great ignorance of those times, when artists did not know the true form of the whale; consider that, as in Perseus's case, St. George's whale may have crawled up out of the sea onto the beach; and consider that the animal St. George rode might have been only a large seal, or sea-horse. With all this in mind, it will not seem altogether inconsistent with the sacred legend and the most ancient drawings of the scene to hold that this so-called dragon was none other than the great Leviathan himself. In fact, set before the strict and piercing truth, this whole story will fare like Dagon, that fish, flesh, and fowl idol of the Philistines: when he was set up before the ark of Israel, his horse's head and both the palms of his hands fell off him, and only the stump, the fishy part of him, remained. So, then, one of our own noble stamp — a whaleman, no less — is the guardian patron of England; and by rights, we Nantucket harpooners should be enrolled in the most noble Order of St. George. And therefore let the knights of that honorable company (none of whom, I venture to say, has ever had anything to do with a whale, as their great patron did) — let them never look down on a Nantucketer, since even in our woolen frocks and tarred trousers we are far better entitled to St. George's decoration than they are.

Whether to admit Hercules among us or not was something I long remained doubtful about. For although, according to the Greek myths, that ancient Crockett and Kit Carson — that brawny doer of joyful good deeds — was swallowed down and thrown up again by a whale, it is still debatable whether that strictly makes him a whaleman. Nowhere does it appear that he ever actually harpooned his fish, unless, indeed, from the inside. Nevertheless, he may be considered a sort of involuntary whaleman; at any rate, the whale caught him, even if he didn't catch the whale. I claim him as one of our clan.

But by the best contradictory authorities, this Greek story of Hercules and the whale is considered to derive from the still more ancient Hebrew story of Jonah and the whale, and vice versa. Certainly they are very similar. If I claim the demigod, then why not the prophet?

Nor do heroes, saints, demigods, and prophets alone make up the whole roll of our order. Our grand master is still to be named; for like the royal kings of old, we trace the headwaters of our brotherhood to nothing less than the great gods themselves. That wondrous Eastern story must now be retold from the Shaster, the Hindu scriptures, which give us the dread Vishnoo, one of the three persons in the godhead of the Hindus — give us this divine Vishnoo himself for our Lord; Vishnoo, who, by the first of his ten earthly incarnations, has forever set apart and sanctified the whale. When Brahma, or the God of Gods, says the Shaster, resolved to re-create the world after one of its periodic dissolutions, he gave birth to Vishnoo to preside over the work. But the Vedas, or mystical books — which Vishnoo apparently had to read before beginning the creation, and which therefore must have contained something in the way of practical hints to young architects — these Vedas were lying at the bottom of the waters. So Vishnoo became incarnate in a whale, and, sounding down in him to the uttermost depths, rescued the sacred volumes. Wasn't this Vishnoo a whaleman, then, just as a man who rides a horse is called a horseman?
Perseus, St. George, Hercules, Jonah, and Vishnoo! There's a membership roll for you! What club but the whaleman's can be headed like that?
